_comment: Factory default permission posture for a PromptAndPray install. `ask` is the desired set that setup/update set-merges into the project's .claude/settings.json; only the rules setup actually INSERTED are recorded in aiwf.config.json._aiwf.ownedAskRules, and an owned rule the operator later removes becomes a tombstone in _aiwf.suppressedAskRules and is never forced back. Foreign rules are never touched.
_allowDenyComment: `allow` and `deny` below are the FACTORY DEFAULT posture, not owned rules: a blanket allow for EVERY shell tool this ruleset gates, with an empty deny, so that protection comes from the explicit ask gate plus the PreToolUse hooks rather than from a brittle command allowlist. Setup applies them only when the project has no permissions block of its own; it never overwrites an existing one.
_shellToolComment: TWO SHELL TOOLS, ONE ASK LIST, AND A BIDIRECTIONAL MIRROR INVARIANT. A permission rule is addressed to a TOOL, and a Windows session carries a `PowerShell` tool next to `Bash`; a list of `Bash(...)` rules alone therefore gated commit/push/reset on one tool and left the other one open, which no wording could fix. So every ask rule below exists TWICE, in the same order: `Bash(<X>)` and `PowerShell(<X>)`. The invariant is checked in BOTH directions by the self-check - every `Bash(<X>)` rule has a `PowerShell(<X>)` mirror, and every `PowerShell(<X>)` rule has a `Bash(<X>)` base - because a one-directional check would tolerate an orphan rule that gates nothing. The same superset argument as `_osComment` covers the cost: a tool a session does not have is a rule that never matches. Gate 4 is wired on matcher `Bash|PowerShell` for the same reason, and the SEMANTICS of the two are not assumed identical - see the hook's header for what PowerShell does and does not document (AST-split subcommands on `;`, `|` and `&&`/`||`, no documented wrapper or `NAME=value` stripping, case-insensitive matching).
_placeholderComment: `<projectRoot>` is rendered by setup from the resolved project root. The three `git -C <projectRoot> ...` forms exist because a -C-prefixed command is a DIFFERENT match string from the bare form, and the push/merge/rebase gate must hold for every form. There is deliberately no blanket -C rule (one matching `git -C` with no verb): it gated every -C form of every git command, read-only ones included, so an ordinary `git -C <another repo> log` raised a dialog while adding nothing to the push/merge/rebase gate the three rendered forms already hold.
_osComment: ONE OS-NEUTRAL SUPERSET, deliberately not a per-OS render: the ruleset ships identically on windows, linux and macos. A rule matches by command prefix, so the Windows-only forms (Remove-Item, del, git.exe) are inert on a POSIX host and the POSIX forms (rm, rmdir, bare git) are inert on Windows - carrying both costs nothing, while an OS-conditional ruleset would add a rendering branch to the one file whose whole job is that a gate is never missing.
_stackComment: The package-manager, migration-tool and container rules are the default set proven in a Node + SQL project. They cost nothing on a project that never runs those commands; the interview may narrow them.
